whatItDoes: Check a sandbox preview on a cron and redeploy it when it has gone down. Fetches the app's health endpoint each run and, on a failure, relaunches it with its database URL and startup secret injected at run time. One deployed copy can watch many apps.
longDescription:
A sandbox preview isn't an always-on host. The sandbox can stay "running" while the app process inside it gets recycled, and the preview URL starts returning 502 until someone redeploys. A plain health-check cron only tells you it's down — it doesn't fix it. This template does the fixing.

On each scheduled run it probes the app's health path (default `/health`, 8-second timeout). If the app responds, the run is a no-op and stops — that guard is deliberate, so it never stacks a second process onto a live one and collides on the port. If the app is down, it re-attaches the sandbox and redeploys the code that's already there, restarting it at the same URL with no human involved.

The target comes from the schedule input, so one deployed copy keeps as many previews alive as you have schedules. When an app needs configuration to come up cleanly, the relaunch env is built at heal time: a port and literal values, an optional `DATABASE_URL` pulled from a Sapiom Postgres handle (`database.get`), and named environment variables the platform injected — never stored in the schedule. Given no target at all, the run provisions a small demo sandbox, deploys a trivial health server into it, and heals that.

You pay for the sandbox itself and for a redeploy only when the app is actually down. The health check between runs is cheap, and a healthy run does no work at all.
notes:
Click **Use this template** — Sapiom builds and deploys it for you, then run it from the workflow page. Your $5 signup credit covers first runs.

Give each run a `sandboxName` and the preview `url` (and usually a `start` command) so it knows what to keep alive. It only heals a sandbox that still exists — the uploaded code is what gets rebuilt. A fully deleted sandbox has to be re-created with a full deploy first; after that, this keeps it up. Any startup secret is named in `injectEnv` (a list of environment variable names) and read at run time from the environment Sapiom injected it into, so the secret never sits in the schedule input.

Prefer to work from the code? Run it locally with `run_local` and `{ "dryRun": true, ... }` to trace the whole heal branch for free — it skips the network probe, assembles the env, and reports the injected env key names without redeploying. Or edit and deploy it with the Sapiom MCP.
